name: retdec
desc: Retargetable machine-code decompiler based on LLVM
why: A retargetable machine-code decompiler from Avast that turns binaries back into readable C, a strong door into reverse engineering.

brief.what_it_is: RetDec is a retargetable machine-code decompiler built on LLVM. It takes an executable or raw machine code and produces readable high-level output, either C or a Python-like language. It handles ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, AR archives, Intel HEX, and raw code, for x86, ARM, MIPS, PIC32, PowerPC, x86-64, and ARM64 (AArch64). Beyond decompiling, it also offers static analysis, compiler and packer detection, a disassembler, call and control-flow graphs, and statistics.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as a decompiler that is 'not limited to any particular target architecture, operating system, or executable file format', so one tool can cover many binary types. The project is from Avast, and the README credits research funding from TACR (Technology Agency of the Czech Republic).
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little detail on internals beyond the feature list. It mentions loading and instruction decoding, signature-based removal of statically linked library code, use of DWARF and PDB debug info, reconstruction of instruction idioms, and recovery of C++ class hierarchies from RTTI and vtables. It also lists C++ symbol demangling for GCC, MSVC, and Borland. Optional UPX unpacking runs in a preprocessing stage.

brief.install_notes: Either download a prebuilt package from the releases page or the nightly TeamCity/GitHub Actions builds, or build from source with CMake. Source builds on Linux need a C++17 compiler (GCC 7 or newer), CMake 3.6 or newer, OpenSSL 1.1.1 or newer, Python 3.4 or newer, autotools, pkg-config, m4, and zlib. Windows needs Visual Studio 2017 or newer and the Visual C++ Redistributable. macOS needs 10.15 or newer and full Xcode, not only the command-line tools. An installed copy needs about 5 to 6 GB of disk. UPX and Graphviz are optional. The README also documents many cmake flags, including -DRETDEC_TESTS=ON, -DRETDEC_ENABLE=<component list>, and -D<dep>_LOCAL_DIR for offline dependencies. The Homebrew formula is not mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: It is retargetable across many formats and architectures, and it outputs C, which is more readable than assembly-like pseudocode. It also reconstructs C++ class hierarchies from RTTI and vtables and can be driven from IDA and radare2 through separate plugins.
brief.status: Limited maintenance mode, per a warning at the top of the README: pull requests are reviewed with priority, issues may wait up to a quarter, and only basic maintenance continues with very limited development. I did not check the latest release or commit date, so I cannot give a date.
brief.caveats: The project is in limited maintenance mode. FreeBSD support is experimental and has no ports package. Docker support is community-maintained. Nightly builds come with no guarantees, and the README warns of possible regressions. The install is large (5 to 6 GB), and building from source needs a substantial toolchain. The wiki is marked 'in progress'. Some documentation and build-artifact links point to Avast's TeamCity server, which I did not test. The README does not describe the license beyond MIT for Avast code, with bundled PeLib under zlib/libpng and third-party licenses listed in a separate file.

judge.reason: RetDec opens a compelling reverse-engineering rabbit hole by reconstructing readable C and C++ structure from binaries across many architectures and formats.

entry.title: RetDec
entry.tldr: A decompiler from Avast that turns compiled executables for many architectures and file formats back into readable C, a hands-on way into reverse engineering.
entry.deeper_look:
RetDec takes an executable or raw machine code and produces high-level output: C, or a Python-like language. It reads ELF, PE, Mach-O, COFF, AR archives, Intel HEX and raw code, for x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64, MIPS, PIC32 and PowerPC. Besides decompiling, it can detect compilers and packers, disassemble, and produce call and control-flow graphs and statistics.

The README describes it as a decompiler that is "not limited to any particular target architecture, operating system, or executable file format". It is built on LLVM, so one pipeline covers many binary types instead of one tool per platform. The project comes from Avast, and the README credits research funding from the Technology Agency of the Czech Republic.

The idea underneath is that a compiler throws information away, and decompiling is the work of guessing it back. The README mentions several of the steps: decoding instructions, stripping statically linked library code by signature, using DWARF and PDB debug info when present, reconstructing instruction idioms, and recovering C++ class hierarchies from RTTI and vtables. Optional UPX unpacking runs first. Reading its C output next to the original binary shows how much structure survives compilation and how much is inferred.

The brew formula also installs a set of helper tools: a file inspector (`retdec-fileinfo`), an unpacker, and utilities for building signature and YARA patterns. These are worth browsing once the main decompiler works.
entry.install:
brew install retdec
# An installed copy needs roughly 5 to 6 GB of disk. UPX and Graphviz are optional extras.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the decompiler's options so you can see what it can be told to do.
Shows the options of the file inspector, which reports on a binary's format, compiler and packer.
Decompiles the binary test.exe into C. The README's example uses this path after a manual install; with brew, run retdec-decompiler directly.

entry.whats_unique: It handles many formats and architectures in one tool and outputs C rather than assembly-like pseudocode. It also rebuilds C++ class hierarchies from RTTI and vtables, and has separate plugins for IDA and radare2.
entry.caveats: The project is in limited maintenance mode, so issues may wait a quarter and development is minimal. The install is large, and the README warns that nightly builds may regress.
